comment.body:
Yours is the only newsletter/Substack I pay for. I read a number of high-quality Substacks, but yours has stood out enough that I wanted to support it. For years, I've relied on your articles to break revelations of the CONVID scam to my readers.

However, the quality of your articles has deteriorated this year. This article is just one of the worst examples.

Given this article's dramatic claims, the fact that you didn't provide links to the studies reported is a big problem. 

So, I asked Claude to find the studies and compare the article to what the studies actually said. I can't paste a screenshot here, so I'll CnP the text, as ugly as it will be. The link to the chat, which is much more readable, is: https://claude.ai/share/13327a60-3d34-4d73-8045-83694f7754df

Claude concluded that neither study bore out the articles claims. Granted, it could only access abstracts (which is all a curious reader would be able to do, also.) If I were an open-minded person who'd been buffaloed by the CONVID nonsense -- which is the kind of person I want to share articles like this with -- my final impression would be that this article is baseless. This would implicate Hulscher and McCullough, as well.

Once you lose credibility, it doesn't matter how stellar your work is. Lack of credibility will render even the best work ineffective. 

I already complained about Frank Bergman's articles consistently stretching the truth and overplaying his hand. It got to the point that I now check who wrote the articles I'm interested in. If Bergman, I save myself the time and skip it.

The kind of misreporting in this article is far worse.

----------------------

Study 1 (Faksova et al., 99 million): PARTIAL ACCURACY
Article Claims:

"500% increased risk of Myocarditis"
"300% increased risk of spinal cord inflammation"

Actual Findings:
The study did find elevated observed-versus-expected (OE) ratios for:

Myocarditis and pericarditis (study confirms increased risk but doesn't report 500% in the abstract)
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM - brain/spinal inflammation): OE ratio 3.78 (278% increase, not 300%) after first dose of mRNA-1273

The study conclusion: "This multi-country analysis confirmed pre-established safety signals for myocarditis, pericarditis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis."

------------------------

Study 2 (Karimi et al., 85 million): MAJOR MISREPRESENTATION
Article Claims:

"300% increased risks of Heart attack"
"200% increased risk of arrhythmias"
"250% increased risk of stroke"

Actual Primary Findings (from abstract):

"No increased risk of heart attack, arrhythmia, or stroke was observed post-COVID-19 vaccination."


"a protective effect on stroke (OR, 0.19; 95% CrI: 0.10–0.39) and myocardial infarction (OR, 0.003; 95% CrI: 0.001–0.006) was observed after the third dose of the vaccine."

What the study actually found:

Overall: NO increased risk for MI, stroke, or arrhythmia
Increased CAD risk: OR 1.70 (70% increase) for second dose specifically
Third dose showed protective effects against stroke and MI
Subgroup analyses showed some elevated risks in specific vaccine/dose combinations, but these were not the primary findings

The article cherry-picked subgroup data while completely omitting the study's primary conclusion that no overall increased risk was observed for these outcomes.

I'm not citing de Tocqueville to praise American democracy.
I cite him as a diagnostic of soft despotism—a precursor to the administrative infantilization you argue is now achieved through rhetoric and spectacle.
Not that you're incorrect, but codependence is a private, interpersonal pathology.
Tocqueville was talking about a structural, administrative one. So it's just a matter of what discipline one cares to see these movements. For me, most times, Im attempting to create an arc from thinkers like Pascal, Nietzsche, Scheler, Cioran, and Tocqueville in an attempt to diagnose the decay of civic life.

comment.body:
I hear ya, but this applies only to people still listening to these professional liars and hoping some sanity will emit from their pie holes. 

"It willingly labors for their happiness..." 

Well, de Tocqueville had an unrealistically rosy view of American democracy, didn't he? It has never done that, although just the little word "own" could correct his statement and expose its naivete: it willingly labors for their *own* happiness -- "them" being those qualifying for inclusion as "people", which in his time was radically different than what people today take the word to mean.

"It would be like the authority of a parent if, like that authority, its object was to prepare men for manhood; but it seeks, on the contrary, to keep them in perpetual childhood."

"Perpetual childhood" = codependence.

Why are epistemics important?

First, because if you don't know how you came to a conclusion, you have no idea whether you can trust the conclusion. The mere fact that you trust it for no known reason says nothing about its trustworthiness. 

Second, because the deplorable fact is: hardly anyone knows or cares how they came to their conclusions. Hardly anyone does anything to figure it out. Even fewer do anything to ensure any figuring out they did made any real sense. In other words: hardly anyone cares about epistemics. 

And that means -- straight up and undeniably -- that their conclusions are, by definition, bullshit.
